Distributed Job Scheduler - HLD

Simulate this design Draw it from memory

Difficulty: Intermediate–Advanced Prerequisites:Message Queues, Leader Election, and Database Indexing

TL;DR

A distributed job scheduler lets teams register recurring or one-off tasks (like cron, but across a fleet of machines). It ensures each job runs exactly once, on time, with retries and dependency management.

In 3 sentences: Users register jobs with a schedule (cron expression) or a one-time fire time. A “ticker” process scans the database for due jobs and enqueues them to Kafka. Worker pods consume from Kafka, execute the job, and report success/failure back. Leader election ensures only one ticker runs per shard.

1. Understanding the Problem

A distributed job scheduler accepts jobs (run once at time T, or recurring on a cron schedule, or a DAG of dependent steps) and executes them reliably across a fleet of workers. Callers shouldn’t worry about which machine runs the job, what happens when a worker crashes mid-execution, or whether the job ran twice. The scheduler owns timing, dispatch, retries, isolation, and observability.💡 A DAG (directed acyclic graph) here just means “a set of steps with dependencies and no loops” — run B after A, run D after both B and C. The no-loops part is what makes a valid execution order always exist. Learn more →

2. Naive First Cut

The 30-second whiteboard version:

Why it collapses under real use:

  • Single point of failure - the one cron loop dies, nothing schedules until someone restarts it.
  • Scheduler and worker coupled - long-running jobs block the schedule tick.
  • No leader election - if you run two cron loops for high availability (HA), both pick up the same due job and run it twice.
  • No retries or backoff - worker crashes mid-run, job is lost.

In simple terms: A worker was running a 4-hour job and crashed at hour 3. Is the job done? Should we retry? If we retry, it runs from scratch - wasting 3 hours of work.

  • Tick granularity - one-per-minute poll can’t handle sub-second precision or 100k due-jobs-per-second bursts.
  • No isolation - a runaway tenant saturates the worker pool, everyone else’s jobs miss their SLA (service-level agreement — the timing promise made to the job’s owner).
  • No observability - “did my job run?” requires grep across worker logs.
  • No dependencies - jobs are independent; can’t express “run B after A finishes.”

The rest of the doc evolves this into a horizontally scalable, HA, exactly-once-in-effect job platform.💡 “Exactly-once in effect” is the honest version of exactly-once: the network can always deliver a message twice, so instead you make the second delivery produce no additional change. Learn more →

Glossary - what these names mean

Quick reference so nothing in this doc is a black box:

Components we build

  • Scheduler API - the HTTP service users call to create, query, cancel jobs.
  • Dispatcher - a process that watches for due jobs and hands them to workers.
  • Hydrator - a background job that copies “soon-due” jobs from the durable DB (Postgres) into the fast in-memory index (Redis), one hour before their fire time. Keeps the hot index small.
  • Sweeper - a background job that finds executions stuck in RUNNING longer than their heartbeat TTL (time-to-live — the age at which we assume the worker is dead) and marks them failed so they can be retried.
  • Worker - a process that picks up a job from the queue, runs the handler code, and reports success/failure.
  • Worker pool - a named group of workers that handle a specific class of jobs (e.g., email-sender, batch-etl).

Infrastructure pieces we use

  • Postgres - relational DB for durable truth. Job definitions, execution history. ACID (a group of writes either all land or none do), SQL queries, easy admin. Learn more →
  • Redis - in-memory data store. We use two structures:
    • Sorted Set (ZSET) - collection where each entry has a score (we use the fire-time timestamp); supports O(log N) range queries by score. Lets us ask “give me all jobs due before now.”
    • Key with TTL - short-lived entries (heartbeats, cancel flags) that auto-expire.
  • Kafka - durable message broker. Topics hold ordered messages; consumers (workers) pull them with per-partition ordering. Used here to decouple dispatch from execution.
  • etcd / ZooKeeper / Consul - distributed coordination services. They store a tiny amount of data very reliably and let N nodes race for a “lease” (temporary exclusive lock). We use them for leader election - picking one dispatcher among N to own a shard.
  • Kubernetes Lease - Kubernetes’ (K8s’) built-in version of the same leader-election idea.
  • Raft / Paxos - consensus protocols that make coordination services (etcd, ZooKeeper) tolerate node failures without split-brain — two nodes both believing they are the leader and each dispatching the same jobs. You don’t implement them; you use a service that does.
  • DLQ (Dead Letter Queue) - a parking spot for messages that failed N retries. Ops reviews them manually.💡 DLQ (Dead Letter Queue) = a holding queue for messages that failed processing after max retries. Operators can inspect and reprocess them later.

External / reference names in Prior Art

  • Airbnb Dynein - Airbnb’s internal delayed-job system.
  • Temporal / Cadence - open-source durable workflow engines (Temporal is the Cadence fork, now the industry standard).
  • Quartz - the classic Java scheduler library with a clustered mode using DB locks.
  • Dkron - a distributed cron daemon built in Go using Raft.
  • AWS EventBridge Scheduler - AWS’s managed version of this entire design.

Observability tools

  • Prometheus - metrics DB. Scrapes services for counters/gauges (e.g., dispatch latency, queue depth), stores time series, powers dashboards and alerts.
  • OpenTelemetry - vendor-neutral SDK that services use to emit metrics, traces, and logs in a standard format.
  • Jaeger - distributed tracing UI. Given a trace ID, shows the full path of a request across services.
  • ClickHouse - columnar analytics DB — it stores each column together on disk instead of each row, so counting failures across a billion executions reads only the status column. Fast at aggregating billions of rows (“how many jobs failed per tenant this week?”); slow at single-row updates. Complements Postgres.

3. Prior Art We’re Drawing From

  • Airbnb Dynein - distributed delayed job queue at Airbnb; uses DynamoDB for job storage, a dispatcher pool that polls by time range, pushes onto SQS for workers. Powers in-app messaging, dynamic pricing. (blog)
  • Uber Cadence / Temporal - durable workflow engine: workflow code runs as a “replayable” function; every step is persisted so the workflow survives host death. Originated at Uber, now the industry standard for multi-step orchestration with human-in-the-loop steps, timeouts, and saga compensation. (Temporal blog)
  • Quartz Scheduler (clustered) - open-source Java scheduler with DB-locked leader election. Classic pattern - a table row with FOR UPDATE or a sentinel column determines the active scheduler. Widely deployed; limits on horizontal scale due to the single write-lock hot row.
  • Dkron - Go-based distributed cron using Raft for leader election. No single point of failure (SPOF), no DB dependency. Good for platform-layer scheduling (host patching, telemetry collection).
  • Google Borg / Kubernetes CronJob - cluster-level job scheduling. Kubernetes CronJob uses a single controller with leader election to create jobs; job pods execute the work.
  • AWS EventBridge Scheduler - the managed version of this pattern at AWS scale. One-shot and cron schedules, EventBridge dispatches to Lambda / SQS / Step Functions. Designed for multi-tenant throughput.

4. Functional Requirements

Core (top 3)

  1. Schedule a job - one-time (run at timestamp T), recurring (cron expression), or delayed (run in N seconds).
  2. Execute reliably - at-least-once delivery to a worker, with retries on failure, respecting timeouts.💡 At-least-once = we keep trying until a worker confirms, and we accept that a job may therefore run twice. Choosing this over at-most-once is the single decision that shapes Deep Dives 2, 3 and 7.
  3. Inspect and cancel - query the status of a scheduled or running job, cancel a future run.

Below the line (out of scope)

  • Workflow DAGs with conditional branches and human steps - that’s Temporal territory; we’d mention it as a deep dive extension.
  • Job output streaming and log aggregation - assume workers ship logs to an existing log pipeline.
  • Cost optimization (spot workers, preemption) - covered in the worker-pool deep dive briefly.
  • Full multi-region active-active - we’ll note what’s needed but design primary-with-DR (disaster recovery — a standby region that takes over if the primary is lost).

5. Non-Functional Requirements

Core

  • Scale - 100M scheduled jobs at rest, 1M jobs/minute dispatched at peak, 10k concurrent executions.
  • Timing precision - P95 (the lateness 95% of dispatches beat) dispatch latency < 1s of scheduled time for “hot” jobs due within the next minute. Best-effort for long-tail jobs scheduled months out.
  • Reliability - at-least-once execution guarantee. Job owners must be idempotent; we provide execution IDs to help them dedupe.
  • Availability - scheduler control plane tolerates single-node and single-AZ (availability zone — one isolated datacentre within a region) failure. No job loss across failover.

Below the line

  • Exactly-once execution end-to-end (impossible; at-least-once + idempotency is the industry standard).
  • Sub-100ms precision for far-future jobs.
  • Strict fairness across tenants (we’ll do weighted, not strict).

6. Scale Estimation (Back-of-Envelope)

  • Users: 10M scheduled jobs at rest, thousands of internal service tenants
  • Write QPS: 1K new job registrations/sec, 1M executions/minute (~16.7K/sec) at peak💡 QPS = queries per second. Note how small the write rate is next to the dispatch rate — this system’s load is dominated by jobs firing, not by jobs being created. Learn more →
  • Read QPS: 10K job status queries/sec, 1K “what’s due now?” sweeps/sec
  • Storage: 500GB job metadata/year (definitions + execution history)
  • Bandwidth: 99.9% on-time execution SLA - dispatch within 1s of scheduled time

7. Core Entities

  • Job - the definition: identity, owner, type (one-shot / cron / delayed), payload, target (worker pool + handler name), retry policy, timeout, priority.
  • Schedule - derived from a Job; holds next_fire_time for cron jobs. Updated after each fire.
  • Execution - one attempt to run a job. Has its own ID, a timestamp, a worker assignment, status (PENDING / RUNNING / SUCCEEDED / FAILED / TIMED_OUT / CANCELLED).
  • Worker Pool - a named group of worker processes that handle a specific class of jobs (e.g., email-sender, batch-etl).
  • Worker - a single process that pulls and runs jobs, sends heartbeats.
  • Tenant - owner of a set of jobs. Quotas and fairness are applied per tenant.

8. API / System Interface

POST   /v1/jobs                     -> Job
  Header: Idempotency-Key: <uuid>
GET    /v1/jobs/:id                 -> Job + latest executions
PUT    /v1/jobs/:id                 -> update schedule or payload

POST /v1/jobs

  "name": "daily-invoice-gen",

  "schedule": "0 3 * * *",
  "timezone": "America/Los_Angeles",
  "target": { "pool": "batch-etl", "handler": "generate_invoices" },
  "payload": { "tenantId": "acme", "dateRange": "yesterday" },
  "retryPolicy": { "maxAttempts": 3, "backoff": "EXPONENTIAL", "initialDelayMs": 30000 },

}
JSON

Response:

{
  "jobId": "job_a93f2",
  "nextFireAt": "2026-05-05T10:00:00Z",
  "state": "ACTIVE"
}
JSON

Security notes:

  • Service JWT on all endpoints; payload is opaque to us.
  • Idempotency key for job creation so retries don’t double-register.
  • Payloads are encrypted at rest - they often carry secrets (API tokens, tenant IDs).

9. High-Level Design

Three passes, one per core functional requirement.

FR1: Schedule a job

New components we need:

  1. Scheduler API - the HTTP interface users call to create, query, or cancel jobs. Validates inputs and stores job definitions.
  2. Postgres (jobs + schedules) - the durable source of truth. Stores job definitions, cron expressions, and computed next_fire_time.💡 We use Postgres because job creation needs ACID transactions - if we write the job and its schedule, both must succeed or neither does.
  3. Redis Sorted Set (upcoming index) - holds jobs due within the next hour, scored by next_fire_time.💡 A sorted set (ZSET) lets us ask “give me everything due before NOW” in O(log N) - the dispatcher polls this instead of scanning millions of rows in Postgres every second.

Step-by-step flow:

  1. Developer calls POST /v1/jobs with a cron expression like "0 3 * * *" (run daily at 3am) → hits the Scheduler API
  2. API validates: Is the cron expression valid? Does the target worker pool exist? Is the payload within size limits?
  3. API computes next_fire_time by interpreting the cron expression in UTC, then writes a jobs row AND a schedules row to Postgres in one atomic transaction
  4. For jobs due within the next hour, API also adds (next_fire_time, job_id) to the Redis sorted set - this is the “hot window” that the dispatcher polls. Jobs further out stay only in Postgres until a background hydrator promotes them
  5. Returns 201 Created with the job ID and next fire time

Why Postgres for jobs: ACID for “create + schedule” atomicity, SQL flexibility for admin queries (“show all jobs by tenant X that fired in the last 24h”), indexes on (next_fire_time, state) for dispatcher polling.

Why Redis ZSET for the hot window: at 1M jobs/min peak, polling Postgres for “jobs due in the next 60s” every second would hammer the index. Redis ZSET gives O(log N) inserts and O(log N + k) range queries by score (timestamp). The ZSET holds only the next hour; everything further out lives only in Postgres, promoted to Redis one hour ahead.

What FR1 leaves broken: the job is durably stored and correctly indexed, and the fire time it computed is wrong for most of the world. Interpreting 0 3 * * * in UTC means a user in Bengaluru who asked for 3 AM gets their job at 8:30 AM local. Deep Dive 4 is where that gets fixed, and the timezone is the easy half — the hard half is what a cron expression means on the two days a year when 2:30 AM local happens zero times or twice. Nothing here fires at all yet either; FR2 builds the dispatcher.

FR2: Execute reliably (the dispatch + retry path)

This is where most of the complexity lives.

New components we need (in addition to the ones above):

  1. Dispatcher - the heartbeat of the system. One process, continuously polling the Redis ZSET for jobs whose fire time has passed.
  2. In-flight set + lease reaper (Redis) - a second ZSET holding jobs the dispatcher has claimed but not yet confirmed onto Kafka, scored by lease expiry. The reaper returns expired entries to the due set.💡 Without this, a dispatcher crash between claiming a job and publishing it drops the job silently, because the claim itself deleted the only record that it was due.
  3. Kafka (per-pool topics) - decouples dispatch timing from worker availability. When the dispatcher finds a due job, it publishes to Kafka rather than directly calling a worker.
  4. Workers - the processes that actually execute your job code. Each worker pool handles a specific class of jobs (e.g., email-sender, batch-etl).
  5. Executions table (Postgres) - one row per attempt to run a job. Append-only history so you can answer “did my job run? when? how long did it take?”
  6. Retry Queue - a delayed Kafka topic where failed jobs wait with exponential backoff before being retried.

Step-by-step flow:

  1. The dispatcher continuously polls the Redis ZSET: “Give me all jobs with score <= now()” - runs every 100-500ms
  2. When it finds due jobs, it claims them with a lease rather than deleting them. One Lua script atomically does ZRANGEBYSCORE on the due set, ZREM from it, and ZADD into an in-flight set scored by now + lease_ms.💡 Deleting outright with ZPOPMIN or ZREMRANGEBYSCORE is the obvious move and it silently drops jobs: the entry is gone the instant it is popped, so a dispatcher that crashes before the Kafka publish loses the job entirely. Leasing keeps the job recorded as “claimed but not yet handed off” until we know it landed. This is SQS visibility timeout, implemented on Redis.
  3. For each claimed job, the dispatcher:
    • Creates an executions row in Postgres with status PENDING
    • Publishes a message to Kafka on the target pool’s topic (e.g., jobs.batch-etl)
    • Only after Kafka acknowledges the write, removes the entry from the in-flight set
    • For cron jobs, computes the NEXT fire time and re-adds it to the ZSET (or Postgres if > 1 hour out)
  4. A lease reaper sweeps the in-flight set for entries whose lease has expired and moves them back to the due set. A dispatcher that died mid-dispatch therefore costs one lease interval of latency, not a lost job.💡 This is what buys the at-least-once guarantee in the NFRs. It also means a job can be dispatched twice — the dispatcher died after Kafka accepted the message but before clearing the lease.
  5. A worker in the target pool picks up the Kafka message and marks the execution as RUNNING
  6. Worker invokes the job handler with the payload - this is where YOUR code actually runs
  7. On success → worker marks execution SUCCEEDED, commits Kafka offset, moves on
  8. On failure → worker marks FAILED, reads the retry policy, and publishes to the retry queue with exponential backoff (30s → 2min → 10min → 1h)

Why lease-and-reap instead of just popping the ZSET? Because Redis is a cache of the hot window, not the ledger, and a pop makes the dispatcher the only place a due job exists. ZPOPMIN and ZREMRANGEBYSCORE both delete the entry the moment it is read, so the gap between claiming a job and Kafka accepting it is a window where a crashed dispatcher takes the job with it. Nothing retries, because nothing knows it was owed. Leasing narrows the failure from “job never runs” to “job runs one lease interval late”, which is the difference between a correctness bug and a latency blip.

And Postgres is the backstop underneath that. The jobs row is the durable source of truth and still carries a next_fire_time in the past, so a slow reconciler scanning for overdue PENDING jobs re-promotes anything that fell out of Redis entirely — a flushed cache, a failed-over replica, a bug in the reaper. Two layers: the lease catches the common case in seconds, the reconciler catches the pathological case in minutes. Never rely on the cache alone to remember that work was owed.

Why Kafka between dispatcher and workers? If the dispatcher called workers directly, a pool restart would lose all in-flight jobs. Kafka gives us durability (messages survive worker crashes), replay (reprocess an hour of jobs if a worker had a bug), and independent scaling per pool.

Why a separate execution row, not just status on the job row: one job may produce many executions (cron fires daily, retries add more). Executions are append-only, cheap to partition by day, and joinable by job_id for history views.

What FR2 leaves broken: the lease makes dispatch durable. Four things it does not make it are fast, available, correct under retry, or recoverable.

  • One dispatcher is the whole scheduling capacity. At 1M jobs/min it is polling, claiming, writing an execution row and publishing to Kafka roughly 16,700 times a second from a single process. Polling latency stretches into seconds, and jobs fire late in a system whose entire purpose is firing on time. Deep Dive 1.
  • One dispatcher is also a single point of failure on the only component that initiates work. It dies at 02:59 and the 03:00 cron wave simply does not happen until someone restarts it. Nothing else in the design notices. Deep Dive 6.
  • A twice-dispatched job runs twice. The lease reaper deliberately re-dispatches a job whose dispatcher died after Kafka accepted the message, which is the right call — losing a job is worse. But nothing downstream can tell the second delivery from the first, so an invoice gets emailed twice. Deep Dive 2 is what makes that re-delivery harmless.
  • A worker that dies mid-job strands its execution forever. The row says RUNNING and no retry is owed, because the only thing that knew the job was in progress was the process that died. Deep Dive 3. And for the 4-hour ETL that crashes at hour 3.5, retrying from zero is its own problem — Deep Dive 7.

FR3: Inspect and cancel

New components we need (in addition to the ones above):

  1. Cancel Set (Redis) - a short-lived set of executionIds that have been cancelled. Workers check this before starting and periodically during execution.💡 We can’t “un-send” a Kafka message, so instead we let the worker check a cancel flag before it starts working. Learn more →

Step-by-step flow (read path):

The read path is straightforward: GET /v1/jobs/:id hits Postgres with an indexed query by job_id - returns the job definition plus recent executions. No drama.

Step-by-step flow (cancellation - the tricky part):

Cancellation sounds simple but has three distinct timing windows:

  1. Cancel a future job (not yet due) - easiest case. API sets the job state to CANCELLED and removes it from the Redis ZSET. It’ll never fire.
  2. Cancel a PENDING execution (dispatched but worker hasn’t started yet) - write the executionId to the Redis cancel set. Worker checks this set before starting; if present, it skips the job entirely.
  3. Cancel a RUNNING execution (worker is mid-flight) - worker polls the cancel set every few seconds during execution. On hit, it sends an interrupt to the handler code. Handlers must cooperate - we can’t force-kill without risking data corruption.

Why lazy cancellation via a flag instead of “delete from the queue”? Kafka doesn’t support targeted message deletion. And even if it did, there’s a race between the cancel request and the worker consuming the message. A cancel flag checked at execution time avoids the queue surgery entirely.

What FR3 leaves broken: the read path is genuinely fine and the honest gap is elsewhere. GET /v1/jobs/:id answers “did this job run” only if you already know which job to ask about. The question an on-call engineer actually has at 3am is “which of our jobs are failing and why”, and answering it here means grepping logs across 200 worker hosts. Deep Dive 8 is about making the system answerable rather than merely correct. Cancellation of a RUNNING execution also stays cooperative: a handler that ignores the interrupt runs to completion, and we accept that rather than force-killing mid-write.

Vendor-agnostic with alternatives listed.

Tier / purpose What it stores Access pattern Primary pick Alternatives

scroll →

Why Postgres and Redis together for scheduling

Postgres is durable truth. Redis is the fast index. The split is the key insight:

  • Far-future jobs (months out) sit in Postgres. We don’t need millisecond access to them.
  • Soon-due jobs (next hour) sit in Redis. Dispatchers poll Redis, not Postgres.
  • A background hydrator job promotes Postgres rows to Redis one hour before their fire time.

This keeps the dispatcher hot path lightning-fast while Postgres handles the scale-at-rest (100M jobs easily on a single partitioned table).

Why not just put everything in Redis?

Redis is not durable at the cost-per-GB point we’re operating at. Losing scheduled jobs on a Redis failover is unacceptable. Postgres plus its write-ahead log (WAL) gives us “if the commit returned, the job will run.”💡 A write-ahead log is a record of every change written to disk before the change itself is applied, so a crashed database can replay it on restart. It is the mechanism behind “the commit returned, therefore it survived”.

Why Kafka for the worker-facing bus?

  • Durability - if workers all restart, messages survive.
  • Per-pool topics - lets us tune partition counts and consumer parallelism per pool.
  • Replay - reprocess an hour of executions if a worker had a bug.
  • At-least-once delivery semantics match our guarantee.

11. Data Modeling

Postgres (Job Definitions — durable truth, sharded by tenant_id):

CREATE TABLE jobs (
    job_id UUID PRIMARY KEY,
    tenant_id UUID NOT NULL,
    name VARCHAR(200) NOT NULL,
    type VARCHAR(15) NOT NULL,    -- ONE_SHOT, RECURRING
    cron_expression VARCHAR(100), -- null for one-shot
    callback_url VARCHAR(500) NOT NULL,
    payload JSONB,
    status VARCHAR(10) NOT NULL,  -- ACTIVE, PAUSED, DELETED
    next_fire_time TIMESTAMP,
    created_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL
);
CREATE INDEX idx_jobs_next_fire ON jobs(next_fire_time) WHERE status = 'ACTIVE';
CREATE INDEX idx_jobs_tenant ON jobs(tenant_id);

CREATE TABLE executions (
    execution_id UUID NOT NULL,
    job_id UUID NOT NULL,
    status VARCHAR(12) NOT NULL,  -- PENDING, RUNNING, SUCCEEDED, FAILED, TIMED_OUT, CANCELLED
    created_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),  -- set at dispatch, never null
    started_at TIMESTAMP,         -- null until a worker picks it up
    finished_at TIMESTAMP,
    worker_id VARCHAR(64),
    attempt_number INTEGER DEFAULT 1,
    error_message TEXT,
    -- Partition on created_at, not started_at: the row is inserted PENDING
    -- before any worker starts, and range partitioning rejects a NULL
    -- partition key. Postgres also requires the partition key in the PK.
    PRIMARY KEY (execution_id, created_at)
) PARTITION BY RANGE (created_at);
CREATE INDEX idx_executions_job ON executions(job_id, started_at DESC);
SQL

Redis (Hot Schedule Index — upcoming jobs ZSET):

Key: "schedule:due:{shard_id}" → Sorted Set (score = next_fire_time_unix_ms, member = job_id)
Contains: only jobs due in the next 60 minutes (hydrated from Postgres by background promoter)
Operations: ZPOPMIN to dequeue, ZADD to schedule

Redis (Worker Heartbeats + Cancellation Signals):

Key: "worker:heartbeat:{workerId}" → Hash { current_execution_id, last_seen_at }
TTL: 30s (auto-expires if worker dies)

Key: "cancelled:{executionId}" → "" (empty value, just existence check)
TTL: 10 minutes

Access Patterns:

Query Data Source How
Create job (one-shot or recurring) Postgres INSERT INTO jobs, compute next_fire_time from cron, schedule if due within 1 hour
Promote upcoming jobs to Redis Postgres → Redis Background job: SELECT job_id, next_fire_time FROM jobs WHERE next_fire_time BETWEEN now() AND now()+1h → ZADD to Redis
Dispatch due job Redis ZPOPMIN schedule:due:{shard} → publish to Kafka execution topic
Execute job Kafka → Worker Worker consumes, checks cancellation set, executes callback, writes result to Postgres
Cancel job Redis + Postgres Add to cancelled:{executionId} set in Redis + update Postgres status
Detect dead workers Redis TTL If worker:heartbeat:{id} expires → re-dispatch its current execution
scroll →

How a Recurring Job Fires Every Hour Without Drift:

  1. Job created with cron 0 * * * * (every hour) → compute next_fire_time = next whole hour
  2. Promoter (runs every 5 min): finds this job in Postgres, ZADD schedule:due:{shard} <next_hour_unix_ms> job_id to Redis
  3. Dispatcher: at the top of the hour, ZPOPMIN returns this job_id → publishes to Kafka
  4. Worker picks up, executes callback URL, writes SUCCEEDED to executions table
  5. Post-execution hook: compute NEXT fire time from cron expression → UPDATE jobs SET next_fire_time = ?
  6. If the execution was slow (took 5 min) → next_fire_time is still the NEXT hour (not now+1h), preventing drift
  7. If worker crashes mid-execution: heartbeat TTL expires → dispatcher detects, re-publishes with attempt_number + 1

12. Deep Dives

The flows above expose the weak spots worth probing. Eight deep dives.

Deep Dive 1 - 1M jobs a minute through one polling loop. Where does the second dispatcher go?

Bad: the single dispatcher FR2 built, polling one Redis ZSET.

  • 1M jobs/min is ~16,700/sec, and each one costs a claim, an execution row, a Kafka publish and a lease clear. One process cannot hold that rate, so the poll loop falls behind and jobs fire seconds late — in a scheduler, which is the one defect users will always notice.
  • You cannot fix it by running a second copy. Two dispatchers polling the same ZSET both see the same due jobs, and the lease only narrows that window rather than closing it. Scaling out requires deciding who owns what first, which is the actual content of this deep dive.

In simple terms: One machine is responsible for checking ‘which jobs need to run right now?’ If that machine gets overloaded, jobs fire late. We need to split the work.

: the single dispatcher FR2 built, polling one Redis ZSET.

One machine is responsible for checking ‘which jobs need to run right now?’ If that machine gets overloaded, jobs fire late. We need to split the work.

: shard the ZSET by . Each shard has its own leader (picked via etcd). N dispatchers poll N ZSETs in parallel.

:

Deep Dive 2 - The reaper re-dispatches a job on purpose. How does the invoice not get emailed twice?

Exactly-once delivery is impossible across a network boundary. The achievable goal: at-least-once delivery + idempotent handlers = “exactly-once in effect.”

Bad: FR2’s worker, which reads the executionId off the message and does nothing with it before invoking the handler.

  • The lease reaper is designed to re-dispatch a job whose dispatcher died after Kafka accepted the message. That is the correct trade — a duplicate beats a loss — so duplicate delivery is a routine event here, not an edge case.
  • The id is present and unchecked, which is the worst of both worlds: it looks like the problem is handled. The worker takes the second delivery, invokes the handler, and the invoice is emailed twice. Nothing in the system records that this execution had already been attempted.
  • The retry queue compounds it. A handler that fails at step 9 of 10 re-runs steps 1 through 8 on the next attempt, so partial side effects are applied repeatedly even without duplicate delivery.

: FR2’s worker, which reads the off the message and does nothing with it before invoking the handler.

: generate an on dispatch. Hand it to the worker. The worker’s first action is to check a “processed” table; if present, skip; else run the handler, record completion.

:

This is the pattern borrowed from Stripe’s idempotency work and Temporal’s activity-retry model.

Deep Dive 3 - A worker dies mid-job. Who notices, and how long does it take?

Bad: FR2’s worker path, where RUNNING is a state nothing ever audits.

  • The worker sets RUNNING, starts the handler, and its pod is evicted. The row stays RUNNING for ever. Nobody retries, because the only process that knew the job was in flight is gone, and the lease reaper does not help — it covers the dispatcher’s crash window, which closed the moment Kafka acked.
  • This fails silently, which is the worst property a scheduler can have. The job did not error and did not alert; it simply never finished, and the first signal is a human noticing a report did not arrive.
  • Pods get evicted routinely — deploys, node drains, out-of-memory (OOM) kills — so at 1M jobs/min this is a steady trickle of permanently stuck executions rather than a rare event.

: FR2’s worker path, where is a state nothing ever audits.

: -based liveness. Workers write to Redis every 10s. A sweeper scans executions stuck in with expired heartbeats and marks them , triggering retry.

:

: worker finished the work but crashed before ACKing. Job effectively ran; our retry will run it again. That’s why the idempotency contract with handlers matters.

Deep Dive 4 - Twice a year, 2:30 AM local either happens twice or not at all. What does a daily cron do?

Bad: FR1’s computation — interpret the cron expression in UTC.

  • A user in India asks for 0 3 * * * meaning 3 AM IST and gets 3 AM UTC, which is 8:30 AM their time. Not late, not drifting: just wrong, every single day, for anyone outside UTC.
  • Storing the offset instead of the zone looks like a fix and is not. IST never shifts, so it would work; America/Los_Angeles moves twice a year, and an offset captured at schedule time is stale the next March.

: FR1’s computation — interpret the cron expression in UTC.

: store . Compute in the user’s zone, convert to UTC for the ZSET score.

:

Deep Dive 5 - One tenant schedules 10M jobs for midnight. Why is that everyone else’s problem?

Bad: FR2’s dispatcher, which pops the ZSET in timestamp order and asks no questions about who owns what.

  • Tenant A schedules 10M cron jobs at 0 0 * * *. At midnight those 10M entries all carry the same score, so they sit at the head of the ZSET as one contiguous block. Tenant B’s single urgent job, due at 00:00:01, is behind all of them.
  • At 16,700 dispatches/sec, draining 10M jobs takes about ten minutes. Tenant B’s job is ten minutes late and tenant B did nothing wrong. Timestamp order is a perfectly reasonable policy that happens to make queue position a function of how many jobs your neighbour scheduled.
  • Per-tenant quotas at submit time do not save you either: 10M jobs spread over a month is well within any sane quota, and they can still all land on the same second.

In simple terms: One customer floods the system with millions of jobs. Other customers’ urgent jobs get stuck behind them. We need fairness - one noisy customer shouldn’t starve others.

: FR2’s dispatcher, which pops the ZSET in timestamp order and asks no questions about who owns what.

One customer floods the system with millions of jobs. Other customers’ urgent jobs get stuck behind them. We need fairness - one noisy customer shouldn’t starve others.

: per-tenant quotas enforced at job-submit time. Cap at N concurrent executions per tenant.

:

Deep Dive 6 - The dispatcher dies at 02:59. What happens to the 03:00 cron wave?

Bad: FR2’s single dispatcher process. Dies → nothing is scheduled until ops restarts it.

  • The answer to the heading is “nothing happens, and nobody is told.” Those jobs do not fail, they do not retry, they simply never fire. Postgres still holds a next_fire_time in the past for every one of them, so the data is there — but no component is looking.
  • Recovery time is human: page, wake, diagnose, restart. Even a good five minutes of that is 5M missed dispatches at peak, and the 03:00 hourly wave is exactly when a scheduler is least able to afford it.
  • Note that Deep Dive 1’s sharding makes this worse before it makes it better: N dispatchers means N single points of failure, each owning a shard nobody else will touch.

: FR2’s single dispatcher process. Dies → nothing is scheduled until ops restarts it.

: two dispatchers with a DB-based lock row (). Quartz’s classic approach.

:

Deep Dive 7 - A 4-hour ETL dies at hour 3.5. Why should the retry start from zero?

Bad: the retry Deep Dive 3 just built, applied to a long job — restart the handler from the top.

  • Correct, and ruinous. The job re-reads the same 3.5 hours of input to get back to where it was, and if the crash cause is environmental (a node that keeps getting evicted) it may never finish at all: each attempt needs 4 uninterrupted hours and the window keeps closing early.
  • There is a second failure hiding underneath. Deep Dive 3’s liveness check assumes a silent worker is a dead worker, and a long job legitimately has nothing to report for minutes at a stretch. Tune the heartbeat tightly enough to catch crashes quickly and you start killing healthy long jobs; loosen it for the long jobs and crashes go unnoticed for just as long. One timeout cannot serve both.

: the retry Deep Dive 3 just built, applied to a long job — restart the handler from the top.

: handlers checkpoint progress periodically. On retry, they read the checkpoint and resume.

:

Deep Dive 8 - “My job ran but the downstream never got the data.” Where do you look?

Bad: what FR2 and FR3 give you — an executions table and GET /v1/jobs/:id.

  • That answers “did job X run”, which is the question you have when you already know the answer is about job X. It does not answer “which of our 50,000 jobs are failing”, “is dispatch latency degrading”, or “this execution succeeded here and the downstream service never saw it, so where did the message go”.
  • The last one is the common support ticket and the executions table is actively unhelpful for it: the row says SUCCEEDED because the handler returned, and everything after that boundary is invisible. Reconstructing the path means grepping logs across 200 worker hosts with no shared identifier to grep for.

: what FR2 and FR3 give you — an table and .

: executions table indexed by job_id. UI shows history.

13. Design Self-Audit

Weak spots checked:

  • Clock skew - dispatcher and workers must agree on “now.” The Network Time Protocol (NTP) keeps hosts in sync; for critical timing we round to the nearest second. Major clock drift would cause duplicate dispatches; fencing tokens (Deep Dive 2) catch those.
  • Redis ZSET size - holding 1 hour of due jobs at 1M/min = 60M entries. One Redis instance can handle that in RAM (~10 GB). For growth, shard the ZSET (Deep Dive 1).
  • Postgres write hot spot - executions table grows fast. Partitioning by month + archive old partitions to S3 keeps the hot table small.
  • Retry storm - a downstream service fails for 5 min, 1M failed executions queue into retry. Retry backoff must be randomized (jitter) and capped; circuit breaker at the worker side pauses retries if failure rate exceeds a threshold.
  • Payload bloat - users pass 10 MB payloads. Cap payload at 256 KB; larger = reference to S3.
  • Dependency on Redis availability - Redis outage = no dispatch. Mitigation: Redis Sentinel / Cluster; cold-start re-hydrates ZSET from Postgres in minutes.
  • Multi-region - primary region in one location, warm standby in another; cross-region Postgres replication (async). On failover, some last-second jobs may re-fire - idempotency catches them.
  • Cost - Kafka and Postgres dominate. Monitor per-tenant cost, bill back for heavy schedulers.

14. Core Flows

Flow 1 - One-shot delayed job (run in 5 minutes)

Walkthrough:

  1. Client posts a job with runAt = now + 5min.
  2. API persists the job and schedule rows, then adds to the Redis hot-window ZSET.
  3. Dispatcher polls the ZSET every 100ms.
  4. At the fire time, dispatcher atomically pops the entry (ZREMRANGEBYSCORE), creates an execution row, and publishes to Kafka.
  5. Worker consumes, marks RUNNING, runs, marks SUCCEEDED, commits.

Non-obvious failure path: if dispatcher crashes between step 3 and publishing, on restart the ZSET entry has already been removed. Safety net: the executions row was created before the publish, so a sweeper sees a PENDING execution with no Kafka publish → re-publishes.

Flow 2 - Recurring cron job with a failure and retry

Walkthrough:

  1. Dispatcher fires the cron job, creates execution e1, publishes to Kafka.
  2. Worker picks up, runs handler, handler throws.
  3. Worker writes FAILED with attempt=1, publishes to retry topic with a 30-second delay.
  4. Dispatcher also advances the next fire time for the cron (+1 day) - retries don’t affect the schedule.
  5. 30 seconds later, the retry topic re-publishes. A worker picks it up as attempt=2.
  6. Succeeds, marked SUCCEEDED.

Non-obvious failure: worker crashes between step 3a (handler throws) and step 3b (publish to retry). Safety net: the execution row is still RUNNING in Postgres. Heartbeat TTL expires in 30s → sweeper marks FAILED_WORKER_LOST → enqueues retry.

Flow 3 - Running execution cancellation

Walkthrough:

  1. Ops calls the cancel API for a running execution.
  2. API writes to a Redis set with a short TTL (10 min is enough; after that the execution is done anyway).
  3. Worker polls the cancel set every 5 seconds (cheap - single GET).
  4. On hit, it sends an interrupt signal to the handler (Java Thread.interrupt, or a cancel-token check in the handler).
  5. Handler cooperatively stops, updates the execution to CANCELLED.

Non-cooperative handlers (native code, infinite CPU loop) can’t be cancelled. We surface that as “best effort” in the docs and kill the worker process after a grace period.

State machine - an execution’s lifecycle

15. Final Architecture

New components:

  • Analytics store (executions OLAP replica): A read-only copy of the executions history in a columnar database, fed by replication from Postgres. It exists because “how many jobs failed per tenant this week” scans millions of rows, and running that query against the live Postgres would compete with the dispatcher writing execution rows 16,700 times a second.

How it works end-to-end:

  1. Client submits job — API call hits the Scheduler API, which persists the job and schedule to Postgres
  2. Hydrator pre-loads hot window — fetches upcoming jobs from Postgres and writes them into Redis ZSET scored by execution time
  3. Dispatcher pops due jobs — leader-elected shard reads from Redis ZSET, acquires shard lock via etcd, updates status in Postgres
  4. Job dispatched to Kafka — dispatcher publishes to the correct per-pool topic based on job type
  5. Worker executes job — each pool consumes only its own topic, so a slow ETL job cannot delay an email send. Workers renew a heartbeat in Redis while running and poll the cancel set
  6. Worker reports completion — writes the result to Postgres; a failure goes back to Kafka for retry and, after the retry budget, to the DLQ
  7. Sweeper catches stuck executions — a worker that dies stops renewing its heartbeat, so the sweeper finds the orphaned execution and re-enqueues it
  8. Metrics and traces exported — Prometheus and OpenTelemetry capture execution latency, success rates, and queue depths

Key Technologies

Term What it is
Redis Sorted Set (ZSET) In-memory data structure scored by fire-time timestamp - O(log N) insert and range queries power the “what’s due now?” dispatcher hot path.
Timing Wheel Alternative scheduling structure with O(1) insert and fire for time-bucketed events - used in some dispatcher implementations for high-volume ticks.
Leader Election Coordination mechanism (via etcd/ZooKeeper/Consul) ensuring only one dispatcher owns each shard - prevents duplicate job firing.
Kafka Durable message broker decoupling dispatch timing from worker execution - survives worker restarts and enables per-pool topic scaling.
Cron Expression Standard syntax (e.g., 0 3 * * *) for defining recurring schedules, parsed with timezone-aware libraries to compute next fire times.
Heartbeat Periodic signal (every 10s) from workers to Redis with TTL - missed heartbeats trigger sweeper-based retry of stuck jobs.
Dead Letter Queue Holding queue for jobs that exhausted all retry attempts - surfaced to an ops dashboard for manual investigation.
Temporal Durable workflow engine for complex multi-step job orchestration with built-in retries, timeouts, and crash recovery.

What’s Expected at Each Level

This section helps you calibrate your depth. You don’t need to cover everything - just know what’s expected for your level.

Mid-level

Design a system that stores jobs with execution times and triggers them when due. Propose a polling mechanism or priority queue for finding due jobs. Understand why a single timer thread doesn’t scale - one machine crashing means jobs don’t fire.

Senior

Propose Redis ZSET for the hot window of upcoming jobs (score = execution timestamp). Explain leader election for preventing duplicate execution across multiple scheduler instances. Discuss retry logic with exponential backoff and dead-letter queues for permanently failed jobs. Articulate the difference between at-least-once and exactly-once execution guarantees.

Staff+

Address multi-tenant fair scheduling (one user’s million jobs shouldn’t starve others) using weighted queues with per-tenant token buckets. Discuss timing wheel data structures for sub-second precision without polling overhead, sharding strategies for the job store (partition by tenant + time bucket), and exactly-once execution guarantees using fencing tokens to prevent stale workers from completing zombie executions.

🎯 Key Takeaways

  • Redis ZSET scored by execution time enables O(log N) “what’s due now?” queries
  • Leader election ensures exactly one worker processes the hot window
  • Dead letter queue catches permanently failing jobs without blocking others
  • Idempotent execution - jobs must be safe to retry

  • Delayed Trigger Service - timing wheels and scheduled execution

  • Zomato - dispatch and async workflows

Related Concepts

Understand the building blocks used in this design:

  • Leader Election → — one scheduler node owns dispatch so due jobs aren’t fired twice
  • Message Queues → — hand due jobs off to a pool of workers for execution
  • Distributed Locking → — narrows a due job to one worker in the common case, but a lease can expire mid-execution, so exactly-once comes from the fencing token plus transactional completion in Deep Dive 2
  • Fencing Tokens → — the monotonic token the downstream store checks, which is what actually makes a duplicate dispatch harmless
  • Dead Letter Queue → — captures jobs that exhaust their retries for later triage

@Ananya Arya, Good catch, you're right. The write-up uses ZREMRANGEBYSCORE rather than ZPOPMIN, but same flaw: it removes the entry before the Kafka publish, so a dispatcher crash in that window loses the job and contradicts the at-least-once guarantee in the NFRs. Fix is to claim with a lease instead of destructively removing. One Lua script does ZRANGEBYSCORE, ZREM from the due set, ZADD into an inflight set scored by now + lease_ms. Remove from inflight only after Kafka acks, and a reaper returns expired leases to due. Basically SQS visibility timeout on Redis. Redis Streams consumer groups give you the same thing via XREADGROUP / XACK / XAUTOCLAIM. Postgres is also a backstop here since it still holds next_fire_time in the past, so a reconciler re-promoting overdue PENDING jobs makes it fire late rather than never.
